name: Gulkand

lead: Gulkand is a jam-like preserve of Damask rose petals and sugar from the Indian subcontinent. In Ayurvedic and Unani practice it is a cooling tonic taken for heat in the body, and people in beauty circles take it hoping that cooling the body translates into calmer, clearer skin.

Research has characterised the rose petals used in Unani preparations such as gulkand, and reviews of edible roses list antioxidant and anti-inflammatory plant compounds. No human trial has tested gulkand for acne, glow or other skin outcomes, so the skin link rests on tradition and on the properties of rose phytochemicals.

paras: It is eaten by the spoonful, stirred into milk or water, or used as a filling in sweets and paan, and is often taken in warm weather. Fans pair it with other cooling foods and a general skin routine.

It is mostly sugar, which matters for people watching sugar intake or managing diabetes. Quality varies between products and rose petals can carry pesticide residue if not organic. It is a food, not a treatment for a skin condition.

angle.text: People take gulkand by the spoonful as part of a skin routine, on the traditional view that its cooling action shows up on the skin. The rose compounds in the petals are the plausible mechanism people point to.

lead: Gulkand, also called rose petal jam, is a sweet preserve from the Indian subcontinent. Its name comes from the Persian words gul (rose) and qand (sugar) [1]. It is traditionally made from Damask roses, although other rose types are also used, and the petals are cooked or sun-cured with sugar until thick [1][2].

In Unani medicine it is used as a cooling tonic, and in Ayurvedic and Persian medicine it is used to help address bodily imbalances [1]. People who use it for their looks follow the traditional logic that a body that runs cooler shows less inflammation and heat in the skin, and eat it as part of a skin-care routine alongside other practices.

Scientific work on gulkand is limited to analysis of its ingredients and to reviews of edible rose flowers, which describe flavonoids, carotenoids and phenolic acids and report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties for roses in general [3][4].

paras: Gulkand is served at room temperature and is made by combining rose petals and sugar, traditionally of the Damask rose [1]. Preparation methods described in reference works include sun-curing the layered mixture or slow-cooking it until the juice thickens [1][2]. It is eaten on its own or used in sweets, drinks and paan.

sections.h: Uses in traditional medicine and beauty
paras: In Unani medicine gulkand is a cooling tonic, and Ayurvedic and Persian traditions use it to address imbalances in the body [1]. A chromatographic study of Unani rose formulations (gulkand, rose water, rose sharbat) describes rose petals as widely used in these preparations for both edible and cosmetic purposes [5]. Users link the cooling idea to appearance, expecting less visible heat in the skin such as flushed, irritated or breakout-prone areas.

No studies found. Related laboratory and review work includes a review of edible rose flowers, which lists gulkand among traditional rose products and reports that rose phytochemicals show antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-aging properties [3], and an HPTLC and GC-MS profiling of rose petals in gulkand, rose water and rose sharbat [5].
